facts.claim: "i've been thinking" is track 8 on Elizabeth's The Wonderful World of Nature Deluxe Edition, and it runs 3:07 on Bandcamp.
The deluxe edition came out on 23 October 2020 through AntiFragile Music worldwide, and through Our Golden Friend in Australia and New Zealand. The original album came out on 1 November 2019.
Elizabeth Mitchell is credited as the composer of "I've Been Thinking" on AllMusic.
The Wonderful World of Nature was produced by John Castle, whose other credits include Hatchie, Angie McMahon, Cub Sport and Vance Joy.
Elizabeth spent the better part of two years on the album and worked with producer and audio engineer John Castle.

The deluxe edition adds seven tracks to the original 11 songs: two piano versions of existing songs, four new songs and a Fleetwood Mac cover. The new additions were recorded in Elizabeth's bedroom during isolation.
Elizabeth said she wanted the album to create a feeling of intense closeness with the listener, as if a trusted friend or conscience were on their shoulder.
The album deals with the end of her marriage. She described reflecting on whether you're the monster or the other person is, rather than casting herself as the victim.
Elizabeth Mitchell fronted the Melbourne indie pop band Totally Mild, which released two albums and disbanded in 2019. The Wonderful World of Nature was her solo debut.
AllMusic describes the album as heartbroken songs about grief, desire and indulgence, set against dense cinematic guitar and synth-pop.

research.lineage: It sits in Melbourne's indie and dream pop scene as a lusher solo pop turn from the former Totally Mild frontwoman, framed as a queer pop anti-heroine heartbreak record.

draft:
The confession comes in the form of a legal defence. "What a chemical thing, I should be let off," the narrator says of the affair at the center of **i've been thinking**, as though desire were a substance that went into the bloodstream without consent. It's a funny line, and a sad one, and it's also not quite meant. The plea for leniency comes right after the narrator admits there was a moment "before when we could have stopped." The narrator knows the exit was there. The chemistry excuse is something said aloud to see whether it holds.

Elizabeth Mitchell wrote the song, and it sits on *The Wonderful World of Nature*, her solo debut after the Melbourne indie pop band Totally Mild split in 2019. She spent the better part of two years on the record with producer John Castle, and AllMusic hears it as heartbroken songs about grief, desire and indulgence set against dense, cinematic guitar and synth-pop. The album turns on the end of her marriage. She has described wanting to ask whether you're the monster or the other person is, rather than playing the victim. This song takes that question at its least flattering angle. The narrator is the one doing the betraying, and the lyrics never pretend otherwise.

The writing works by repetition. "I've been thinking" opens line after line like a person circling the same memory in bed at night: the touch, the friendship, the way the other person moved. Then the questions start, and they're asked half to the lover and half to the narrator's own conscience. "Would you do it again? I would" asks, then answers before the other person can, so nobody else gets a say. There's a "she" in the third verse, someone who may or may not have known what was going on, and she gets one line before the song turns back to the two people in the room.

The final stretch is where the feeling sharpens. "Is it terrible that I don't care?" sounds at first like a request for absolution. A few lines later the question has become a statement, and "I" has become "we," a shared shrug in place of a private doubt. The guilt hasn't gone anywhere. It has been outvoted. What's left is the image the song keeps returning to, hands in hair, and the last word is about wanting rather than remembering.

That fits the closeness Mitchell said she wanted from this record, the sense of a trusted friend or a conscience sitting on your shoulder. Here the conscience is present and gets heard out, and then it loses anyway. The song doesn't ask the narrator to be good, and it doesn't ask you to forgive. It asks you to recognise the pull.

The hook is the honesty of "I would": the song lets you stand inside a choice you might condemn from outside, and feel exactly how good the bad thing was.
